corrected_value.authors: Magnuson, J. S., McMurray, B., Tanenhaus, M. K., & Aslin, R. N.
corrected_value.title: Lexical effects on compensation for coarticulation: The ghost of Christmash past.

decision.location: Section 3.2 Results and Discussion; Section 5 General discussion; References (lines 4, 581-588)
decision.quote: We observed robust LCfC when we combined items that survived our pilot criteria in our experiments: Lexically restored phonemes influenced perception of subsequent phonemes (e.g., a shift toward more  tapes  responses following  fooli#  vs. more  capes  responses following  Christma# ). Critically, participants in our experiment only ever heard ambiguous phonemes at the ends of context stimuli, suggesting that phoneme restoration was driven by the lexicon rather than by experiment‐induced biases (the explanation McQueen et al.,  2009  proposed for the results of Magnuson et al.,  2003a ). We observed LCfC effects both in an initial experiment  and  in a direct replication of the study, with effect sizes comparable to those reported by Elman and McClelland ( 1988 ) and Magnuson et al. ( 2003a ).
decision.reason: The paper conducts two preregistered experiments (an initial study and a direct replication) testing lexically mediated compensation for coarticulation (LCfC) using only ambiguous context-final phonemes specifically to test whether the LCfC finding of Magnuson et al. (2003a) holds without the experiment-induced bias confound proposed by McQueen et al. (2009), and explicitly compares the observed 7% and 6% LCfC effects against the 6% effect reported by Magnuson et al. (2003a) as well as updating their transitional-probability corpus analysis. The reference list (lines 581-588) identifies Magnuson, J. S., McMurray, B., Tanenhaus, M. K., & Aslin, R. N. (2003a), 'Lexical effects on compensation for coarticulation: The ghost of Christmash past', Cognitive Science, 27(2), 285-298 (distinct from their 2003b commentary). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 626) is Elman & McClelland (1988, doi: 10.1016/0749-596x(88)90071-x, Journal of Memory and Language), which is a separate earlier study by different authors; report equivalence does not apply. No prior adjudication or state file exists.

decision.quote: The purpose of this research was to conduct a practice-based replication of Academic and Behavior Combined Support (ABC Support), a previously developed and experimentally evaluated supplemental intervention that merges a combined focus on reading fluency and academic engagement.
decision.reason: The source text available to the blind coder is an abstract reporting a single-case practice-based replication of the previously developed and experimentally evaluated Academic and Behavior Combined Support (ABC Support) intervention by the same author team (Gettinger, Kratochwill, Levin, Eubanks, & Foy). Because only the abstract was available, the blind coder left the bibliographic fields empty. Shipped row input_row_index 1563 (Gettinger, Kratochwill, Eubanks, Foy, & Levin, 2021, 'Academic and Behavior Combined Support: Evaluation of an integrated supplemental intervention for early elementary students', Journal of School Psychology, doi: 10.1016/j.jsp.2021.09.004) is that exact original evaluation of ABC Support. No prior adjudication or state file exists.

decision.quote: The present study reports on a replication of the technical adequacy of the Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire (SSWQ), which is a 16-item self-report instrument for assessing youth’s academic efficacy, educational purpose, joy of learning, and school connectedness, with a sample of adolescents in Grades 6 to 7 ( N = 438).
decision.reason: The source text is an abstract by Tyler L. Renshaw reporting a replication of the technical adequacy and latent factor structure of the 16-item Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire (SSWQ) in a sample of 438 adolescents. Because only the abstract was available, the blind coder left the original study's bibliographic fields blank. Shipped row input_row_index 712 (Renshaw, Long, & Cook, 2015, 'Assessing adolescents’ positive psychological functioning at school: Development and validation of the Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire.', School Psychology Quarterly, doi: 10.1037/spq0000088) is the original development and validation study of the SSWQ whose psychometric properties are retested here. No prior adjudication or state file exists.

decision.quote: Using 2007–2013 data from the United States, research by Fitzgerald, Schor, and Jorgenson lent support to this policy option by finding a positive and statistically significant relationship between average work hours and state-level CO2 emissions. We replicated their analyses by including more recent data and confirmed the linkage between the average hours worked in a state and annual overall CO2 emissions.
decision.reason: The abstract explicitly states that the authors replicated the analyses of Fitzgerald, Schor, and Jorgenson on the relationship between average working hours and state-level CO2 emissions in the United States (originally using 2007-2013 data) by including more recent data (2014-2017). The blind coder only had the abstract and therefore recorded only the author surnames 'Fitzgerald, Schor, and Jorgenson' without year, title, or DOI. Shipped row input_row_index 47 (Fitzgerald, Schor, & Jorgenson, 2018, 'Working Hours and Carbon Dioxide Emissions in the United States, 2007–2013', Social Forces, doi: 10.1093/sf/soy014) is that exact original study. No prior adjudication or state file exists.

corrected_value.title: Psychological Examining in the United States Army.

decision.reason: In addition to replicating Stephen Jay Gould's (1981) undergraduate administration of the Army Beta (represented by shipped row input_row_index 1094 and blind target_index 0), the authors empirically re-analyze two original correlation matrices of World War I draftee Army Beta subtest scores (n = 693 on p. 390 and n = 1102 on p. 634) from Yerkes (1921, reference [15]: Yerkes R.M., 'Psychological Examining in the United States Army.', Government Printing Office, 1921) using confirmatory factor analysis (Tables 4 and 5) to test the robustness of the original test creators' claim that the Army Beta subtests measure a single general cognitive ability against a two-factor alternative separating subtests with written numbers. Yerkes (1921) is the primary historical psychometric report of the World War I Army testing program and is completely distinct from Gould's book (the sole shipped row, input_row_index 1094); report equivalence does not apply. No prior adjudication or state file exists.
